title: Nu metal
wiki_lead:
Nu metal (sometimes stylized as nü-metal, with a metal umlaut) is a subgenre of alternative metal that combines elements of heavy metal music with elements of other music genres such as hip-hop, funk, industrial, and grunge. Nu metal rarely features guitar solos or other displays of musical technique and emphasizes rhythm with instrumentation that is heavily syncopated. Nu metal guitarists often use seven-string guitars that are down-tuned to produce a heavier sound. Vocal styles are often rhythmic and influenced by hip-hop, and include singing, rapping, screaming and sometimes growling. DJs are occasionally featured to provide instrumentation such as sampling, turntable scratching and electronic background music. Nu metal is one of the key genres of the new wave of American heavy metal.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, bands like Pantera, Helmet, and Faith No More were influential in the development of nu metal with their groove metal and alternative metal styles. Korn is often credited as pioneering the subgenre in the mid-1990s with their self-titled debut album. Nu metal became popular in the late 1990s, with bands and artists such as Korn, Limp Bizkit, and Slipknot all releasing albums that sold millions of copies.
Its popularity continued through the early 2000s, with bands such as Papa Roach, Staind, and P.O.D. all selling multi-platinum albums. The popularity of nu metal came to a peak in 2001 with Linkin Park's diamond-selling debut album, Hybrid Theory. By the mid-2000s, however, the oversaturation of bands, combined with the underperformance of several high-profile releases, signaled the subgenre's decline. Many nu metal bands disbanded or changed their sound in favor of other genres. Genres such as metalcore and emo overtook nu metal in popularity.
The 2010s brought a nu metal revival; many bands that combined it with other genres (for example, metalcore and deathcore) emerged, and some nu metal bands from the 1990s and early 2000s returned to the nu metal sound. Bands such as Of Mice & Men, Emmure, Issues, My Ticket Home, Bring Me the Horizon, and Motionless in White combined nu metal with metalcore or deathcore. Artists like Grimes, Poppy, and Rina Sawayama integrated nu metal sounds into electronic pop music in the late 2010s and early 2020s, and interest in nu metal rose in the early 2020s.

Terminology and origins
Nu metal is a subgenre of alternative metal. Sometimes stylized as nü-metal, the genre has also been dubbed aggro-metal or simply aggro. MTV states that the early nu metal group Korn "arrived in 1993 into the burgeoning alternative metal scene, which would morph into nü-metal the way college rock became alternative rock." Stereogum similarly said that nu metal was a "weird outgrowth of the Lollapalooza-era alt-metal scene". grok_lead: Nu metal is a subgenre of heavy metal music that emerged in the mid-1990s, blending elements of alternative metal, hip-hop, and grunge to create a raw, aggressive sound often centered on themes of personal trauma, alienation, and rebellion. Pioneered by bands like Korn, whose self-titled 1994 debut album introduced downtuned guitars, hip-hop-inspired rhythms, and emotionally charged vocals, the genre quickly gained traction among suburban youth seeking an outlet for angst. It achieved massive commercial success in the late 1990s and early 2000s through acts such as Limp Bizkit, Linkin Park, Slipknot, and System of a Down, selling millions of albums and dominating rock radio and festivals. The origins of nu metal trace back to the early 1990s California underground scene, influenced by rap-metal pioneers like Rage Against the Machine and earlier crossovers such as Anthrax's 1991 collaboration with Public Enemy, as well as extreme metal bands including Pantera and Sepultura, and 1990s hip-hop artists like N.W.A. and the Geto Boys. Korn's October 11, 1994, release, recorded at Indigo Ranch Studios in Malibu, California, became a cornerstone, eventually selling over 10 million copies worldwide and inspiring a wave of imitators. The genre's rise accelerated with the 1998 album Follow the Leader by Korn and the 2001 launch of Kerrang! TV in the UK, which amplified its visibility, leading to a peak in popularity from 1997 to 2001 marked by multi-platinum records and headlining spots at events like Ozzfest. By the mid-2000s, nu metal declined due to market oversaturation, the rise of emo and indie rock, and backlash against its often macho, gimmicky elements, including controversial lyrics and fashion like baggy pants and backward caps. Key characteristics include groove-heavy riffs, turntable scratching, simple verse-chorus structures, and a mix of screamed and rapped vocals that emphasized emotional vulnerability over technical virtuosity. Other prominent bands, such as Deftones, P.O.D., and Static-X, expanded its scope, incorporating nu-metal into broader alternative sounds and achieving widespread cultural impact through MTV videos and soundtrack placements. In the late 2000s and 2010s, nu metal saw a revival through newer acts like Bring Me the Horizon and Issues, blending it with metalcore and electronic elements, while nostalgia-fueled reissues and tours sustained interest into the 2020s. As of 2025, the revival continues with new releases from veteran bands like Linkin Park and P.O.D., and tours such as the Nu Metal Revival Tour. This resurgence forms part of a broader rock and metal revival, featuring nu-metal and raw rock resurgence led by veteran artists like Deftones setting the pace for newcomers.
